title: Cloud Computing: An Overview
topics: Cloud Deployment Models (Public, Private, Hybrid, Community)
AI and Big Data in Cloud

bullets.text: Introduction to cloud computing, its meaning, importance, features, models, advantages, challenges, and applications.
Goal is to provide a clear understanding of cloud computing's role in the digital world.
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet.
Services include servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and AI.
It's a way of renting computing resources instead of buying and maintaining them locally.
Analogy: paying for electricity without owning the power plant.
Makes technology more affordable, scalable, and convenient.
On-demand self-service: users access resources without human interaction.
Broad network access: services available over the internet from various devices.
Resource pooling: providers share resources across multiple customers while keeping data isolated.
Rapid elasticity: resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.
Measured service: usage is monitored and billed according to resources consumed.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): delivers fundamental computing resources like virtual machines, storage, networking (e.g., AWS EC2).
Platform as a Service (PaaS): delivers infrastructure plus a development platform with built-in tools (e.g., Google App Engine).
Software as a Service (SaaS): delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet, accessed via a browser (e.g., Gmail, Microsoft 365, Zoom).
Public Cloud: services delivered over the internet, shared by multiple organizations, cost-effective and scalable.
Private Cloud: dedicated to a single organization, offers more control and security but can be more expensive.
Hybrid Cloud: combines public and private clouds to balance flexibility with security.
Community Cloud: shared by several organizations with common goals or requirements (e.g., healthcare, education).
Reduces costs by eliminating heavy investment in hardware, maintenance, or data centers.
Improves scalability, allowing businesses to easily expand or reduce resources.
Enhances flexibility, enabling access to applications and data from anywhere.
Provides reliability through backup, disaster recovery, and high availability.
Supports innovation by allowing faster experimentation and deployment without infrastructure limits.
Security and privacy concerns due to data being stored on remote servers.
Downtime risks, as services depend on internet connectivity and outages can affect access.
Compliance issues for industries with strict regulations on data storage.
Vendor lock-in, making it difficult and costly to switch providers.
Performance concerns for applications requiring very high processing speed or low latency.
Common applications include data storage/backup, business collaboration, entertainment, healthcare, education, and research.
Cloud computing supports AI and big data analytics by providing high-performance computing resources on demand.
Edge computing processes data closer to the source to reduce latency, relying on the cloud for storage and management.
Future trends include multi-cloud strategies to avoid vendor lock-in and improve reliability.
Serverless computing allows developers to focus on code while the cloud provider manages infrastructure.
Continued focus on security, compliance, and integration with AI, blockchain, and 5G.
